walkthroughs.body_html:
Changing Cities — a core area of GCSE Geography.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Changing Cities brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Changing Cities.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between random, stratified and systematic sampling?
options: Random: every member has equal chance of selection. Systematic: pick every nth item. Stratified: divide the population into groups and sample proportionally from each — ensures subgroup representation.
All three sampling methods produce the same results.
Thermohaline circulation is driven by the wind blowing across the ocean surface.
Stratified sampling means picking samples from different strata of rock.
Meanders form because the river is going downhill very steeply.
Differences in seawater density driven by BOTH temperature (thermo) and salinity (haline) — cold, salty water sinks at high latitudes, driving a global ocean conveyor belt over centuries.
Thermohaline circulation is driven by the wind blowing across the ocean surface.
Thermohaline circulation is driven only by temperature differences in the ocean.

mcqs.q: Why do meanders migrate across a floodplain?
options: Faster water on the outside of the bend causes erosion (river cliff); slower water on the inside causes deposition (slip-off slope) — over time the channel shifts laterally.
Meanders form because the river is going downhill very steeply.
Thermohaline circulation is driven by the wind blowing across the ocean surface.
Meanders form because rivers flow around obstacles like rocks.
